passage:
For more than a century, the keepers of a lighthouse on the north shore of Lake Superior wrote down the weather every few hours. [Their logbooks, now stored in a state archive,] record wind direction, wave height, and the color of the sky at dawn. To the keepers, these notes were routine. Similarly, to climate scientists today they are treasures.

Historians first noticed the logbooks' value in the 1990s, when a graduate student digitizing old shipping records found that the keepers' entries matched storm reports from passing freighters. Unlike a freighter, the logs offered something the ships could not: an unbroken record from a single place. A ship passes through a storm in a few hours, but a lighthouse stays where it is, and it does not move, season after season.

Turning handwritten notes into usable data has proven slow work. Each keeper had a personal shorthand. One wrote "NW fr" for a fresh northwest wind; another simply drew an arrow. Volunteers now transcribe the pages online, and each page is checked by at least two different people before its numbers are added to the database.

The effort is already paying off. Comparing the keepers' records with modern measurements, researchers have figured out that the lake now freezes, on average, about two weeks later than it did a century ago. The keepers, who never imagined their notes would be read this way, simply wanted to keep the light burning and the ships safe. Their careful habits have given scientists a rare gift: a long view of a changing lake.

The first time I paddled the Clearwater River with my aunt Rosa, I spent most of the trip staring at the bow of my kayak. Rosa, [who has guided rafting trips for twenty years] kept telling me to look up. "The river is talking," she said. "You just have to learn it's language."

Over the next summer, I began to understand what she meant. Between two submerged rocks lies the safest channel, marked by a smooth V pointing downstream. A V pointing upstream warns of a hidden boulder. Waves that curl back on themselves, called holes, can trap a boat, even a skilled paddler avoids them. Reading these signs quick became a habit; by August I was calling out hazards before Rosa did.

Kayaks can be made of plastic, fiberglass, or wood. Rosa taught me to check the gauge reports each morning, because a river that rises a foot overnight can, in a very short amount of time, transform a gentle stretch into a dangerous one. She kept a notebook of water levels going back a decade, and she could predict, almost to the hour, when the spring melt would peak.

On my last trip of the season, Rosa let me lead. I chose our line through every rapid, and twice I steered us around holes that were near the left bank. Watching me pick a line through the last rapid, a grin spread across Rosa's face. At the take-out, she handed me her notebook. "You'll need this more than I will," she said. I still have it. Its pages are filled with numbers, and in every one I can hear the river talking.

For more than a century, the keepers of a lighthouse on the north shore of Lake Superior wrote down the weather every few hours. Their logbooks, now stored in a state archive, record wind direction, wave height, and the color of the sky at dawn. To the keepers, these notes were routine. Similarly, to climate scientists today they are treasures.

Historians first noticed the logbooks' value in the 1990s, when a graduate student digitizing old shipping records found that the keepers' entries matched storm reports from passing freighters. Unlike a freighter, the logs offered something the ships could not: an unbroken record from a single place. A ship passes through a storm in a few hours, but a lighthouse stays where it is, and it does not move, season after season.

Turning handwritten notes into usable data has proven slow work. Each keeper had a personal shorthand. One wrote "NW fr" for a fresh northwest wind; another simply drew an arrow. Volunteers now transcribe the pages online, and each page is checked by at least two different people before its numbers are added to the database.

The effort is already paying off. Comparing the keepers' records with modern measurements, researchers [have figured out] that the lake now freezes, on average, about two weeks later than it did a century ago. The keepers, who never imagined their notes would be read this way, simply wanted to keep the light burning and the ships safe. Their careful habits have given scientists a rare gift: a long view of a changing lake.

When the Westbrook Public Library added a seed library in 2019, the librarians were not sure anyone would use it. The idea was simple: patrons could [check up] a packet of seeds in spring, grow the plants, and return seeds saved from the harvest in the fall. The library's first catalog listed forty varieties, most of them donated by a single retired farmer.

The first spring, only a dozen patrons borrowed seeds. Therefore, by the next year, word had spread through the town's garden club and its two elementary schools, and more than three hundred packets went out. Both schools science teachers, in particular, found that a packet of bean seeds could anchor a whole unit on plant life cycles. Students who planted the seeds at home bringing their harvests back to class in September.

Not every packet came back as hoped. Gardeners discovered that some vegetables, such as squash, cross-pollinate easily, so seeds saved from them may not grow true to the parent plant. Seeds from these plants can produce offspring that are different from the plants they came from. The librarians responded by labeling each packet "easy," "medium," or "advanced" to save, and the farmer's beans, which reliably breed true, became the most popular "easy" choice.

Today the seed library circulates more than a thousand packets a year. It's shelves hold heirloom tomatoes, drought-tolerant peppers, and a variety of corn which was grown by the founders of the town and which had nearly been lost entirely. No one at the library still wonders whether patrons will use the seeds.
hints: What do library patrons do with books they borrow?
teaching_explanation: Borrowing an item from a library is to "check out" the item.
strategy_explanation: Supply the idiom yourself, then match.
remember: Phrasal verbs change meaning with the small word.

distractors.rationale: "Check up" means to investigate, not to borrow.
"Check over" means to inspect.
"Check off" means to mark an item on a list.

strategies.explanation: Supply the idiom yourself, then match.

For ninety years, a ferry has crossed the harbor between Port Ellery and Gull Island every night at eleven. The boat itself [had changed] several times; the current one, the blue-hulled Marguerite, entered service in 1998. Its schedule, however, has not. Riders say the night ferry is as dependable as the tide. On a calm night the crossing takes twenty-two minutes, and the lights of Gull Island grow from a faint smudge into a row of windows along the pier.

Most of the late-night passengers are workers. Among them is nurses finishing hospital shifts, cooks from the restaurants along the waterfront, and a baker on who the island depends for its morning bread. The captain, Lou Petrakis, knows most of them by name. He keeps a thermos of coffee in the wheelhouse for regulars and a box of spare gloves for anyone who forgets a pair in winter.

Running a ferry at night is harder than daytime. Fog rolls in without warning, and the harbor's buoys, which are only dimly lit at night when it is dark, can be hard to see. For this reason, Petrakis has memorized the channel so thoroughly that he says he could steer it with his eyes closed, though he has never tried.

Last spring the city proposed ending the night run to save money. More than two thousand residents signed a petition against the plan, and the nurses' union argued, that cutting the route would leave hospital workers with no way home after late shifts. At a public hearing, the baker brought a loaf of bread for every member of the council. In June the city reversed course. The ferry still leaves at eleven.

Twice a month, during the lowest tides, a group of volunteers gathers on the rocks below Point Harlan with clipboards and measuring tapes. They are counting sea stars[, the] task is slower than it sounds. Each animal must be found, measured, and checked for signs of the wasting disease that killed millions of sea stars along the Pacific coast beginning in 2013.

The survey was started by Lena Ashby, a marine biologist which teaches at the community college nearby. When the disease first appeared, she realized that no one had kept careful records of how many sea stars lived at the point before the outbreak. Without those numbers, it was impossible to say how much had been lost. She resolved that if another outbreak came, there would be a baseline.

The volunteers range from retirees to high school students. Most had never seen, a sea star up close before joining, and Ashby trains them in a single afternoon. Two people looking at the same pool, she has found, rarely count exactly the same number of animals. For this reason, she insists that every count be checked by a second person.

The work has already paid off. In 2021, the volunteers noticed young sea stars in pools where none had been seen for years. Because the survey had begun well before the recovery, Ashby had the numbers to measure it. By the time she published her report in 2023, the number of juveniles has tripled since the first sightings. A finding she later shared with researchers at three universities.

Ashby says the most important quality in a volunteer is not expertise but patience and the patient ability to wait calmly. The volunteers records now fill eleven binders, and she hopes they will someday make dull reading: a long, uneventful list of healthy sea stars.

Its bronze pointer, called a gnomon, had been bent sideways years earlier[—probably by a falling branch, and] its shadow pointed nowhere near the right hour.

Last spring our science club decided to fix it. The club had less than forty dollars in their account, so we asked the hardware store on Main Street for help. The owner was nice about it and helped us out a lot, and our adviser, Ms. Varga, found an old diagram of the dial in the school archives.

[5] To set the angle, we needed: a protractor, a level, and a magnetic compass.

We bent a new rod to 42 degrees, aimed it at true north, and bolted it in place. On the first sunny afternoon, therefore, the shadow still read about an hour behind the library clock. Every April, about two hundred volunteers staff the water stations along the Harbor City Marathon. For the past three years, I [have been] one of them, and I have learned that handing a cup of water to a stranger who is running past is harder than it looks.

Our station sits at mile eighteen, the point where many runners begin to tire. Our captain, a retired nurse named Delia Moss, placed us in pairs in the narrow gap among two long tables and told us to hold each cup either by its base or to pinch it near the top. [1] The first runners reached us at 9:40. [2] By noon our tables were sticky, our shoes were soaked, and we had handed out more than eleven thousand cups. [3] They were the elite athletes, moving so fast that most of them never slowed down. [4] Behind them came thousands of others, in various different kinds of conditions. 

Around one o'clock, a runner in a faded green shirt stopped at our table, drank two cups, and asks whether she was still on pace to finish before the course closed. Delia checked her watch and told her yes, as long as she kept moving. The runner thanked Delia and I and set off again at a slow, steady jog.

I never learned whether she made it. Still, when the results were posted that evening, I caught myself scanning the list for a runner in a green shirt, which is not, it turns out, something a results list records.

Every weekday morning in Mumbai, India, roughly five thousand delivery workers known as [dabbawalas, collect] home-cooked lunches from kitchens across the city. By lunchtime, each meal has reached its owner's desk, often many kilometers away, and by evening the empty containers are back home. The service began in the 1890s, and today it handles more than a hundred thousand lunches a day.

A single lunchbox, or dabba, usually passes through several hands. A collector picks it up from a home, often by bicycle, and carries it to the nearest railway station. There, the boxes are sorted by destination; then loaded onto commuter trains. At the other end, another worker picks them up and delivers them on foot or by handcart.

To keep track of so many boxes, the dabbawalas rely on a simple code of colors, numbers, and letters painted on each lid. The code shows where a box started, which station it is going to, and which building it must reach. Because the code is so simple, mistakes are more rarer than an outsider might expect.

The dabbawalas—most of whom come from farming villages outside the city, share their earnings within small groups and settle most problems among themselves. They use no computers or tracking devices. Nevertheless, their lunches arrive consistent on time, even during the city's heavy monsoon rains.

Business schools and companies around the world have studied the system, and visitors often ask to follow a lunchbox along its route. For the dabbawalas, though, the measure of success remain simpler: a customer whose lunch arrives warm and on time.

On January 15, 1919, people in Boston's North End heard a sound like machine-gun fire. The rivets of a huge steel tank near the harbor were popping loose. The tank [held: well over] two million gallons of molasses, and within seconds all of it was pouring into the streets.

When the engineer Washington Roebling became too ill to visit the construction site of the Brooklyn Bridge, the work did not stop. Instead, messages traveled back and forth [between he] and the site through a single person: his wife, Emily Warren Roebling.

Washington had developed a crippling illness in 1872 after working in the caissons, the pressurized chambers sunk into the riverbed to build the bridge's foundations. For years afterward he laid in a room overlooking the river, following the work as best he could from a distance.

In the summer of 1858, a long spell of hot weather turned the River Thames into something close to an open sewer. Since 1800, London's population had [grew] to well over two million, and most of the city's waste flowed, by way of old drains and overflowing cesspool's, straight into the river. Newspapers soon gave the season a name: "the Great Stink."

Doctors at the time disagreed about what caused the city's repeated cholera outbreaks. Many blamed a poisonous "bad air" rising from filth, while a few argued that the disease spread through contaminated drinking water. Either way, the remedy pointed in the same direction: get the sewage out of the river.

Parliament, whose building stands beside the Thames, could hardly ignore the problem; lawmakers reportedly soaked the curtains in chemicals to block the smell. Within weeks, they passed a law giving the city's Metropolitan Board of Works the power and the money to act.

The board's chief engineer, Joseph Bazalgette, already had a plan. He proposed large intercepting sewers that would run alongside the river and catch waste before it reached the water. The sewers would carry the waste east. They would carry it to outfalls downstream of the city. Because much of the land was too flat for gravity alone to keep the flow moving, the system also needed four, large, pumping stations to lift the sewage. Bazalgette also planned for a city larger than the one he saw. 

London's population today is more than three times as large as it was in 1858, and many of Bazalgette's tunnels still carry its waste. One of the original pumping stations, at Crossness, have been restored, and visitors can tour its ornate iron engine house.

One night in 1936, the story goes, he looked at two folding chairs in his office and imagined them on wheels. With the help of a mechanic named Fred Young, he built a folding metal frame that held two baskets, one above the other.

Goldman introduced the carts in his stores in 1937, expecting shoppers to love them. To his surprise, the carts were almost used by no one. Many men said that pushing a cart made them look weak, and many women said that they had pushed enough baby carriages already.

Later inventors improved it; one version could slide into the cart in front of it, so carts no longer had to be folded and stored. passage:
Supermarkets sell many different kinds of food. Yet the cart was invented less than a century ago, by a grocer in Oklahoma City, Oklahoma who owned a chain of stores called Humpty Dumpty.

In the 1930s, shoppers carried wire or wicker baskets, and many stopped adding items being that the baskets grew too heavy. The grocer, Sylvan Goldman, noticed the problem. One night in 1936, the story goes, he looked at two folding chairs in his office and imagined them on wheels. With the help of a mechanic named Fred Young, he built a folding metal frame that held two baskets, one above the other.

Goldman introduced the carts in his stores in 1937, expecting shoppers to love them. To his surprise, the carts were [almost used by no one]. Many men said that pushing a cart made them look weak, and many women said that they had pushed enough baby carriages already.

Goldman refused to give up. He hired people to push carts around his stores and pretend to shop, and he stationed an employee at the entrance to offer each customer a cart.  Without his persistence, shoppers might of kept lugging baskets for years.

Irregardless of the early complaints, stores across the country soon began to adapt the cart. Later inventors improved it; one version could slide into the cart in front of it, so carts no longer had to be folded and stored. Today carts come in many forms: small ones for children; long, narrow ones for crowded city stores; and motorized ones for shoppers who have trouble walking.
hints: Which word does "almost" describe?
teaching_explanation: "Almost" should modify "no one" (nearly nobody used them), so it goes right before "no one."
strategy_explanation: Put the modifier next to the word it limits.
remember: Place limiting words like almost, only, and nearly right before what they limit.

distractors.rationale: "Almost used" means the carts were nearly but not actually used, which is not the intended meaning.
This word order is ungrammatical.
The comma breaks up the phrase, and "almost" still does not clearly modify "no one."

strategies.explanation: Put the modifier next to the word it limits.
